extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of Popular Science Monthly and scientific practitioners (botanists, physicists, chemists, physicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply substantive criteria and explanatory standards used in a 19th-century Popular Science Monthly issue for judging scientific definitions, experimental devices (batteries), and medical/physical explanations in popular-science essays and correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant-individual definition (phyton-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A plant individual is that smallest part that can grow when separated from its former place in a plant community, and given the fitting conditions for growth by itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and elaboration: in most cases this "smallest part" is the phyton or a portion of the stem with its leaf and the bud or growing point in its axil; a young lateral bud is the vitalized undeveloped stem; if there are two buds on the phyton there are two individuals (two distinct points of growth). Use this definition when identifying the unit of a higher plant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell as unit for non-phyton plants
rubrics_metrics.description: "The unit of growth is the cell; in it, either alone or in connection with other cells, all the functions of life are performed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this criterion for lower plants and unicellular organisms: where no phyton elements exist the individual may be a single cell (yeast, bacteria, desmids, diatoms). When cells form filaments or laminae, recognize degrees of independence and division of labor; the seat of individuality is the localised protoplasm capable of growth and reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protoplasm seat-of-vitality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The seat of vitality is protoplasm, and wherever there is enough of this vitalized substance to grow and reproduce its kind, there we have an individual."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess individuality by the amount and distribution of protoplasm: concentrated in a single cell or distributed through many cells. Increased division of labor complicates recognizing individuals; nevertheless an individual consists of a mass of protoplasm (in one or more cells) capable of independent growth and eventual reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of secondary battery (functional definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "By a secondary battery is meant a galvanic battery which, as at first put together, has no tendency to give a current at all; but, if a current of electricity be passed through it of sufficient tension to decompose the fluids which it contains, will give a current in the opposite direction, due to the recombination of the separated parts of the decomposed fluid."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this operational definition when classifying electrochemical devices; the account contrasts primary (yielding current by chemical combination) and secondary (charged by current and later yielding current by recombination) batteries. Historical examples: platinum or lead plates, Plante's spiral lead plates, Faure's red-lead coated plates with absorbent felt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish stored-energy form (chemical separation vs electrical strain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condenser/Leyden-jar stores energy as electrical molecular strain, whereas Faure's secondary battery stores energy as chemical separation (potential energy that can become kinetic e.g., heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or evaluating 'electric storage' be precise about the physical form of stored energy; avoid loose nomenclature that conflates electrostatic strain with chemically stored potential energy. The page urges public scientific leaders to explain the real state of things to prevent confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery performance criteria: internal resistance and surface area
rubrics_metrics.description: Low internal resistance (large surface area) is required so that a battery will "give for a short time what practical electricians call a quantity current."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate battery designs by internal resistance and effective surface area (Plante's spiral to increase surface and lower resistance). Low resistance enables high short-term currents; capacity/duration also depends on plate formation and chemistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery capacity and formation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Plante increased the time for which the battery would yield a given current (its capacity) by an elaborate process of "formation" — charging and discharging with varying direction and leaving the battery undisturbed for gradually increasing intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging battery capacity, consider whether the manufacturing/formation process increases usable capacity and at what extra expense or complexity; Faure's innovation claims to increase capacity without lengthy formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/commercial evaluation of energy-storage inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial questions: cost of the battery, durability, convenience, and suitability for specific use-cases (e.g., storing feeble power over long time for later quick use, temporary electric light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to theoretical performance, judge inventions on practical metrics: first cost, maintenance, weight/bulk, safety (no noxious fumes), availability of charging sources (dynamos, engines), and whether they are economically preferable to alternatives like primary batteries or transmission by wire for given scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of technology for use-case (portage vs conduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare portability of batteries (conveying stored energy by moving batteries) versus conduction through wires; a method is judged by whether it provides a means of 'porterage superior to conduction' for the intended application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the metaphor in the discussion: battery-cans vs fixed pipes. Evaluate on relative efficiency, convenience, and where infrastructure (wires/pipes) can or cannot be laid; do not expect a portable storage method to supplant conduction where conduits are practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regenerative-storage application criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable property of storage for vehicles: ability to store energy developed by the vehicle when running downhill for reuse on ascents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing storage systems for transportation, include capability for recuperation (storing braking/regeneration energy) and how that affects practical utility for electric railways or carriages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary-battery evaluation for fuel substitution (coal/coal-gas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion for a primary battery using coal/coal-gas: must give a good proportion of the theoretical energy of the fuel and have manageable internal resistance; if internal resistance is high it is difficult to use, but Faure's secondary batteries might collect and store the feeble current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider theoretical energy recovery, electrical characteristics (internal resistance), and how secondary storage can compensate for feeble but prolonged primary outputs in particular use patterns (e.g., daily electric lighting needs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy criterion for geological/hydraulic explanations (spouting springs)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation must account for observed intermittent/sudden spouting; gradual compression of gas as water rises would produce uniform flow, not intermittent spouting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed mechanisms against observed dynamics: does the mechanism explain the suddenness and intermittency? If not, it is inadequate. Use analogies (air-chamber of a force-pump) to test plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical-vibration therapeutic apparatus requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of apparatus required "admit of considerable variety, providing only that due rapidity of motion and shortness of stroke were preserved."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or assessing vibration therapy devices for neuralgia or pain control, ensure adequate frequency (rapidity) and short stroke; variety of mechanical forms is acceptable but these parameters are essential for efficacy according to the correspondent's experimental experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical efficacy and dose-response for vibration therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal of pain is progressive, and the anaesthetic effect increases with increase of rate of mechanical vibration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess therapeutic claims against observed progressive/graded responses; evidence-based evaluation should note rate-dependent effects and report reproducible outcomes (e.g., control of neuralgia, insomnia, potential for painless surgery under sufficient conditions). Also consider proposed physiological mechanisms (transmitted energy increasing oxidation, removing congestion, functional revulsion) as explanatory, but require empirical confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis-test compatibility criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed mechanism (e.g., Boudet de Paris's fixed-rate opposition of abnormal nerve vibrations) must be compatible with observed facts (observed progressive increase of anaesthesia with vibration rate challenges a fixed-rate hypothesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating explanatory hypotheses, check that the model's predictions match experimental observations; if key observations contradict the hypothesis, the hypothesis should be revised or rejected.
